'''Dame Kathleen Mary Ollerenshaw''', {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|DBE}} (''née'' '''Timpson'''; 1 October 1912 – 10 August 2014) was a British mathematician and politician who was [[List of lord mayors of Manchester|Lord Mayor of Manchester]] from 1975 to 1976 and an advisor on educational matters to [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s government in the 1980s.

==Early life and education==
She was born Kathleen Mary Timpson in [[Withington]], Manchester, where she attended [[Lady Barn House School]] (1918–26).<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2014/aug/12/dame-kathleen-ollerenshaw|title=Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw obituary|first=Norman|last=Clarke|date=12 August 2014|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref> She was a grandchild of the founder of the [[Timpson (retailer)|Timpson]] shoe repair business, who had moved to Manchester from [[Kettering]] and established the business there by 1870.<ref>{{cite book |title=Manchester Memoirs |first=Kathleen |last=Ollerenshaw |publisher=E. J. Morton |year=1982 |page=6}}</ref> She became fascinated with mathematics, inspired by the Lady Barn headmistress, Miss Jenkin Jones. While at Lady Barn, she met her future husband, Robert Ollerenshaw.

Ollerenshaw became completely [[deaf]] at age eight and was taught to [[lip reading|lip read]].  She gravitated toward the study of [[mathematics]] as it is not dependent on hearing.  She was further inspired by a headmistress at Lady Barn House School who studied mathematics at [[Cambridge University|Cambridge]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kathleen Ollerenshaw - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Ollerenshaw/ |access-date=2022-03-05 |website=Maths History}}</ref>

As a young woman, she attended [[St Leonards School]] and Sixth Form College in St Andrews, Scotland where today the house of young male boarders is named after her. At the age of 19 she gained admittance to [[Somerville College, Oxford]], to study mathematics. She completed her doctorate at Somerville in 1945 on "Critical Lattices" under the supervision of [[Theodore William Chaundy|Theo Chaundy]]. She wrote five original research papers which were sufficient for her to earn her [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] degree without the need of a formal written thesis.<ref>[http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/ollerenshaw.htm Dame Kathleen Timpson Ollerenshaw], ''Biographies of Women Mathematicians'', online at [[Agnes Scott College]] site</ref>

While an undergraduate, she became engaged to Robert Ollerenshaw, who became a distinguished military [[surgeon]] ([[Colonel (United Kingdom)|Colonel]] R.G.W. Ollerenshaw, ERD, TD, BM, DMRD)<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/40395/supplement/627/data.pdf|title=Supplement to the London Gazette|date=28 January 1955|website=Thegazette.co.uk|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/44053/supplement/7949/data.pdf|title=Supplement to the London Gazette|date=15 July 1966|website=Thegazette.co.uk|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/36786/supplement/5135/data.pdf|title=Supplement to the London Gazette|date=10 November 1944|website=Thegazette.co.uk|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref> and a pioneer of [[medical illustration]]. They married in September 1939 and had two children, Charles (1941–99) and Florence (1946–72). In 1942 she suffered a [[miscarriage]] and "cried nonstop for three days" as a result of stress when her husband was posted abroad for front-line [[World War II|war]] service.<ref>{{cite news|title=Centenarian Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw – Conqueror of Magic Squares, Rubik's Cube and Mauna Kea|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/dame-kathleen-ollerenshaw/|work=[[Scientific American]]|publisher=[[Nature Publishing Group]]|date=18 September 2012}}</ref>

==Career==
After the Second World War, the Ollerenshaws moved to Manchester, where Kathleen worked as a part-time lecturer in the [[School of Mathematics, University of Manchester|mathematics department at Manchester University]] while raising her children and continued her work on lattices. In 1949, at the age of 37, she received her first effective hearing aid. 
[[File:Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw MAS 2007.jpg|thumbnail|right|Kathleen Ollerenshaw, aged 95, at Manchester Astronomical Society in 2007]]

Outside of academia, Ollerenshaw served as a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] councillor for [[Rusholme]] for twenty-five years (1954–1979), a member of the city council's finance committee (1968–1971), a chairman of the education committee of the Association of Municipal Corporations (1967–1971), Lord Mayor of Manchester (1975–1976), [[High Sheriff of Greater Manchester]] from 1978 to 1979, and the prime motivator in the creation of the [[Royal Northern College of Music]]. She was made a [[Freedom of the City|Freeman of the City]] of Manchester and was an advisor on educational matters to [[Margaret Thatcher]]'s government in the 1980s.

She was President of the [[Institute of Mathematics and its Applications]] from 1978 to 1979.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.ima.org.uk/about_us/institute_history/ima_presidents.cfm.html | title=IMA Presidents | publisher=[[Institute of Mathematics and its Applications]] |year=2014 | access-date=4 August 2014 }}</ref> She published at least 26 mathematical papers, her best-known contribution being to [[Magic square|most-perfect pandiagonal magic squares]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ima.org.uk/publications/|title=Category : Publications|website=ima.org.uk|date=12 April 2023 }}</ref> Upon her death, she left a legacy in trust to support distinguished research visitors and public engagement activities at the [[School of Mathematics, University of Manchester]]. An annual public lecture at the university is named in her honour.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mims.manchester.ac.uk/events/ollerenshaw-lectures/|title=Ollerenshaw lectures – The University of Manchester – School of Mathematics|publisher=University of Manchester|access-date=9 March 2007|archive-date=6 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120206230756/http://www.mims.manchester.ac.uk/events/ollerenshaw-lectures/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
 
An amateur astronomer, Ollerenshaw donated her telescope to [[Lancaster University]], and an [[observatory]] there bears her name. She was an honorary member of the Manchester Astronomical Society and held the post of vice-president for a number of years.

Ollerenshaw attended [[St Leonards School]] in [[St Andrews]], Fife, and served as the school's president from 1981 to 2003. She was succeeded by [[Hazel Byford, Baroness Byford|Baroness Byford]], [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] spokeswoman in the [[House of Lords]]. She [[centenarian|turned 100]] in October 2012.<ref name="Centenary">{{cite web|title = The 2012 Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw Lecture|work = News|publisher = [[University of Manchester]]|date = 3 October 2012|url = http://www.manchester.ac.uk/aboutus/news/display/?id=8777|access-date = 3 October 2012}}</ref>

She died in [[Didsbury]] on 10 August 2014, at the age of 101.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/dame-kathleen-ollerenshaw-former-lord-7597607 | author=Emma Flanagan | date=12 August 2014 | access-date=12 August 2014 | newspaper=[[Manchester Evening News]] | title=Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw former Lord Mayor of Manchester dies aged 101 }}</ref> Her husband and both their children had predeceased her.

==Honours and legacy==
* In 1970, Ollerenshaw was appointed [[Order of the British Empire|Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] for services to education.
* Composer Sir [[Peter Maxwell Davies]] dedicated his [[Naxos Quartets|Naxos Quartet No. 9]] to her.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.naxos.com/catalogue/item.asp?item_code=8.557400|title=DAVIES, P.M.: Naxos Quartets Nos. 9 and 10 (Maggini Quartet) - 8.557400|website=Naxos.com|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref>
